body:
Continuing the inquiry, I take the account, the objection, and the rival as three partially successful probes. I would not discard any of them, but I would not keep the account's ordering. The objection is right that the account's central ambiguity hypothesis is not the only reading of 'we agreed and later disagreed about what it meant.' The same fact can be renegotiation under changed shifts, a dispute about who has standing to enforce a term, or a symptom of load imbalance. The account's own o1 admitted this, then continued as if the ambiguity reading had priority. That priority is not earned by the material. I also accept the objection's claim that the recurrence test is weak: if specified chores stop recurring, that is compatible with several mechanisms, and recurrence may simply migrate to new items or return at the next schedule change.

The rival adds a second axis that the account and the objection both underplay: the dispute may be about what the flat is, not only about what the chores mean. On that reading, writing down done-ness criteria is not a neutral clarification; it enacts a unit-with-obligations picture that one flatmate may be avoiding. I take that as a live hypothesis, not a conclusion. The rival's own warning is important: the privacy/constitution reading can pathologize any explicit expectation and shield a flatmate who simply will not do a fair share. So it should not become the new default either.

What I would use: the account's practical suggestions, but demoted to probes. The objection's demand that alternative hypotheses be treated as rivals and that the test be built to distinguish them. The rival's separate conversations, its attention to whether the flatmate engages with content or pulls back from the proposal itself, and its truce-shaped options such as owned zones or default rotations. What I would reject: the account's sequence that begins with a shared written note and treats the living-arrangement question as a late threshold; the objection's occasional slide toward treating ambiguity as merely a sequencing error rather than a genuinely possible diagnosis; and any use of the rival reading to rule out making expectations explicit at all.

The revised approach I would try:

1. Do not open with a shared specification document. Ask the other two, separately, two concrete things: what they want the flat to be (a shared project with obligations, or private lives that overlap in a kitchen), and what specifically makes the chore conversations hard. Ask as a real question, not a survey whose answers will be aggregated into a settlement. Keep the conversations separate at first. This is the rival's diagnostic move, and it also serves the objection's demand to put the conversational-form reading nearer the front.

2. Watch what happens when formalization is proposed, not only what is said about chores. If the withdrawing flatmate engages with the content of a proposed criterion — 'the bins should be out by Tuesday night, but my shift makes that hard' — that supports the ambiguity or renegotiation readings. If they pull back from the idea of any binding arrangement, that supports the constitution or conversational-form readings. If they say they are tired of being the one who notices, that supports load imbalance. These are not decisive, but they are more discriminating than recurrence alone.

3. Run small, reversible probes rather than one household protocol. For a possible ambiguity problem, try a minimal spec on one or two items: what counts as done, by when, and what happens if someone cannot do it. For a possible constitution problem, try owned zones or a default rotation that nobody has to negotiate in the moment. For a possible form problem, change the setting: no group meeting, no moral language about 'pulling weight,' maybe an asynchronous note. For a possible load problem, track who notices and who initiates, not only who performs the task. Use one or two probes at a time so the response is informative.

4. Set out in advance what would count against the ambiguity reading: recurrence stops on the specified items but fresh complaints appear elsewhere; recurrence returns after the next schedule change; the withdrawing flatmate disengages more when specifications are proposed; the same person continues to carry the noticing and initiating. If those happen, do not keep tightening the spec. Shift the inquiry toward load, legitimacy, conversational form, or the living arrangement.

5. If the avoidance continues after a few low-pressure attempts and one or two concrete arrangements, then the question is no longer primarily about chores. That does not mean the withdrawing flatmate is the problem; it means the arrangement may not fit. Raise the lease-and-living-arrangement question explicitly rather than letting a chore dispute decide it by attrition.

What remains open: which hypothesis is actually dominant, what the recurring chores are, what the withdrawing flatmate has said, and whether any written arrangement would be experienced as a truce or as an imposition. The material does not settle those. The next useful move is not to choose a side but to gather the missing information in a way that lets the rival readings show themselves.

owned zones or default rotations with no audit for constitutional/privacy concerns; asynchronous or narrowly scoped talks for conversational-form concerns.","action":"Run one or two probes at a time, on one or two concrete recurring items, and observe which hypothesis the response fits.","depends":["n1","n4"],"consequence":"Keeps the inquiry diagnostic and avoids treating one reading as already settled."},{"id":"n9","type":"commitment","text":"If the withdrawing flatmate pulls back when formalization is proposed, stop pushing written specifications as the primary remedy and shift to conversational form and household-constitution questions.","scope":"Contingent on n7 or n8 being tried.","action":"Change the intervention, not merely the wording of the same specification demand.","depends":["n7"]},{"id":"n10","type":"commitment","text":"If recurrence falls on specified items but fresh complaint items appear, or recurrence returns after the next schedule change, treat that as evidence against the pure ambiguity hypothesis and investigate load imbalance, renegotiation, or legitimacy.","scope":"Contingent on a specification probe being tried.","action":"Do not count a temporary fall in recurrence as confirmation of the ambiguity reading.","depends":["n2"]},{"id":"n11","type":"problem","text":"The material does not identify the recurring chores, the history of the disputes, what the withdrawing flatmate has said, or which of the live hypotheses is dominant;
